To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) high Na+ intake increases blood pressure, body weight and albuminuria and reduces insulin sensitivity in Type 2 diabetes; (2) these responses are greater in diabetic patients with micro- than in those without albuminuria; and (3) insulin resistance could contribute to the greater salt sensitivity and albuminuria observed in diabetic patients with albuminuria.
high salt intake increases blood glucose and albuminuria and decreases insulin sensitivity and renal haemodynamics in Type 2 diabetes patients.
high Na+ intake increases blood pressure, albuminuria and body weight, in Type 1 diabetic patients with micro albuminuria, and this is related to increased insulin resistance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of sodium on blood pressure and urinary albumin excretion in patients with type 2 diabetes.
the role of insulin sensitivity in the pathogenesis of salt sensitivity and microalbuminuria in Type II diabetes.
the effect of sodium intake in Type 2 diabetes and its relationship with insulin resistance, albuminuria and glomerular pressure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results indicate that high salt intake increases blood glucose levels in Type 2 diabetes, and that insulin resistance could be a factor in this increase, but the results are not sufficient to draw any conclusions about whether insulin resistance contributes to the increased blood pressure and albumuria in Type 1 diabetes.
the effect of salt on albuminuria is mediated through blood pressure and insulin sensitivity.
the effect of sodium intake on albuminuria is dependent on renal haemodynamics and insulin sensitivity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

in diabetic patients with microbuminuria, high sodium intake may contribute to the worsening of albuminuria by increasing glomerular pressure, and insulin resistance may play an important role in this phenomenon.
insulin resistance is associated with increased glomerular filtration pressure and albumin excretion in diabetic patients with micro-albuminuria.
insulin resistance could be one of the mechanisms by which high salt intake causes albuminuria in diabetes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
high salt intake is associated with insulin resistance in diabetic patients with micro albuminuria.
high salt intake increases the risk of developing diabetic nephropathy.
high-salt diet increases albuminuria in diabetic patients with micro-albuminuria, and this is associated with insulin resistance.
